A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, What Matters in Data for DPO? All main-text and appendix material is readable and supports comparison. The additional page in v3 reflects reference pagination, not missing or newly added scientific material.

before.justification: v2 reports original DPO training experiments in Section 5, including response-quality comparisons, online DPO versus continual SFT, preference-gap counterfactuals, and data-mixture results in Tables 1–4.

after.justification: v3 retains the original experiments and results in Section 5 and Tables 1–4, together with the reward-model versus LLM-judge selection comparison described in Appendix B.1.

M1.justification: The DPO objective, fixed-chosen online DPO setup in Section 4.2, and data-generation procedure in Algorithm 1 are unchanged. The new PILAF passage describes prior work rather than a modification to this work's methods.

E1.justification: Both versions use Open Assistant 2 and UltraFeedback for training and retain evaluation on AlpacaEval-2, MMLU, IFEval, TruthfulQA, and GSM8K. The response-quality, preference-gap, and on/off-policy mixture scenarios are unchanged.

E2.justification: The SFT baseline and online DPO versus continual SFT comparisons in Tables 1–2 are unchanged, as is the selection-method comparison in Appendix B.1. PILAF is newly cited but is not evaluated.

E3.justification: Section 5.1 and Appendix B retain the same model checkpoint, filtering procedures, dataset sizes, training settings, mixture ratios, and evaluation metrics and protocols. No experimental setting is revised.

E4.justification: The chosen/rejected quality analyses, preference-gap counterfactuals, on-policy mixture experiments, and Appendix B.1 reward-model selection analysis are retained without additions or revisions.

E5.justification: Both versions state in Section 5.1 that benchmark results average three independent runs with different random seeds. Uncertainty reporting and statistical procedures are unchanged.

E6.justification: All numerical entries in Tables 1–5 are unchanged, including benchmark outcomes and dataset statistics. The qualitative findings in Section 5 and Appendix B.1 are also identical; Table 3's relocation introduces no new results.

T1.justification: Theorems 4.1, 4.3, and 4.5, Propositions 4.2 and 4.4, their assumptions, and the Appendix A derivations are unchanged. The PILAF discussion adds no mathematical result or proof to this work.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same claims about chosen-response quality, contrastiveness, and the relationship between fixed-chosen online DPO and SFT. No contribution is added, strengthened, or narrowed.

C2.justification: Interpretations concerning chosen-quality dominance, limited benefits from changing rejected responses, and quality-dependent benefits of on-policy data remain unchanged. Appendix B.1 retains the same qualifications about reward-model scores.

D1.justification: Appendix B retains identical generation parameters, training hyperparameters, evaluation instructions, hardware specifications, and runtime information. Code and data access information is unchanged.

R1.justification: Section 3 adds Feng et al. (2025), PILAF, and a corresponding reference. The new passage connects PILAF's policy interpolation and gradient alignment to this paper's focus on data-dependent optimization, providing a limited expansion of research positioning.

P1.justification: v3 adds a short PILAF discussion to the on-policy related-work paragraph and updates the corresponding author's email. The remaining prose and section organization are retained.

P2.justification: Table 3 moves from page 9 to page 10, other tables shift vertically, and references extend onto a nearly empty page 14. Figure 1, table structures, and captions are unchanged; appendix rendering differs only in page numbers.

improvement.justification: The added PILAF discussion in Section 3 makes the connection to related work on sampling distributions and optimization more explicit, modestly improving scholarly context. The scientific evidence and reproducibility information remain unchanged, so the benefit is limited; the pagination changes do not materially impair comparison or readability.
